AMENDMENT RESPECTING PREVENTIVE DETENTION OF SEXUAL OFFENDERS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-189, to amend the Criminal Code (preventive detention of sexual offenders).

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PREVENTIVE DETENTION OF SEXUAL OFFENDERS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PREVENTIVE DETENTION OF SEXUAL OFFENDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to deal with a problem which became apparent in the Supreme Court of Canada decision in the case of Klippert v the Queen. The court decided that under the present wording of a section of the Criminal Code a homosexual might be held in preventive detention for life if he were likely to commit the offence again.
The majority of the court said the wording of the section as at present in the code would have that result. A minority of the court, of which Chief Justice Cartwright was one, held that the real intent of parliament was that this should only apply in the case of a dangerous offender. The purpose of this bill is to amend the law to make it comply with the view of the minority of the court.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, December 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Trudeau for the second reading of Bill No. C-187, respecting divorce.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure whether you can hear my voice but I will do my best. Last night when I was speaking in this debate I sought to outline in general terms the main objection which I and some others have to the bill we are discussing. This objection is that it fails to accept a new approach to the question of determining the proper basis for divorce, that new approach being by way of marriage breakdown.
May I turn now to discuss the present bill in the light of the general observations I have made. The main provisions of the legislation are contained in clauses 3 and 4. Clause 3 provides that adultery, cruelty and certain other matters shall be grounds for divorce. Cruelty includes both mental and physical cruelty so as to "render intolerable the continued cohabitation of the spouses." It is fairly obvious that if the breakdown principle were adopted such a situation would be clear evidence of marriage breakdown and the petitioner would be able to obtain a divorce on that ground without specially naming cruelty. Clause 3 retains as a ground for divorce the commission of the act of adultery. Under the breakdown theory, if it were adopted, it might well be that an act of adultery or continued acts of adultery would form the basis of a breakdown of a marriage. However, there might well be circumstances in which the commission of an act of adultery would not be sufficient ground for saying a marriage had broken down. There seems little reason why the law should concentrate on such a superficiality, if I may use such language about conduct which is clearly wrong and which may, indeed, wreck a marriage. But, after all, it is a wrong which is nearly always a symptom rather than the cause of the failure of a marriage.
If the law is amended as proposed by the minister we shall continue under the new law to hold trials based upon contrived hotel and motel assignations. This will continue to be the easiest way to secure a divorce. Its
Divorce Law Reform
popularity, in the sense of its frequent adoption, will continue, and I suggest the abuses attached to it will remain.
Clause 4 pays lip service to the idea of the breakdown of a marriage as a ground for divorce. It lists a number of situations which are said to constitute a permanent breakdown. However, it will be noted that subclause 2 provides that a permanent breakdown of a marriage is deemed to have been established when any of the circumstances named in subclause 1 are shown to exist.
Perhaps the minister will tell us later whether this is intended to be what lawyers call an irrebuttable presumption. I assume it is. In other words, once any of these circumstances has occurred it is presumed that the marriage has broken down. If this is the proper interpretation, and I believe it is, what is the purpose of referring to permanent breakdown at all? The individual paragraphs themselves spell out the circumstances which are the basis for divorce. May I point out that these specific headings make no provision for other circumstances not listed which may cause the breakdown of a marriage. They therefore restrict the courts on occasions when the courts should, I suggest, grant a divorce-cases in which the marriage is clearly dead but the circumstances do not fit into the pigeonholes of the bill.
On the other hand, the clause presumes the irreparable breakdown of a marriage whenever any of a list of circumstances exist. This is quite apart from any marriage breakdown. Imprisonment for a long period may well lead to a marriage breakdown, it is true, but I cannot understand why imprisonment alone, unaccompanied by evidence of marriage breakdown, should be a proper ground for divorce.
One of the unfortunate features of the bill before us is that it continues all of the present rigmarole which lawyers know as the three C's-collusion, connivance and condonation. These are the formulas whereby the dissolution of a marriage can be refused on the ground that the parties have agreed to it, have forgiven an act of misconduct complained of or have encouraged its commission. I believe all lawyers familiar with divorce cases are well aware of the farce which is carried on in the courts whereby a petitioner for divorce is drilled to repeat a firm denial that he has offended against this formidable though somewhat unintelligible legal proposition.

December 15, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
The bill goes even farther. I do not know whether it intends to do so, but I invite the attention of the minister and the house to clause 9 which provides that it shall be the duty of the court to refuse a decree based upon the consent of the parties. In the context it may have been intended that this should refer to formal, written consent. But it might well be interpreted by the courts to mean that where the parties have consented to a divorce or to the circumstances upon which the divorce is based, a decree must be refused.
Take the question of separation. Suppose the parties have been separated for not less than three years, as mentioned in the bill. Such a separation might obviously be the subject of consent. Indeed, it could be the subject of legal agreement, and the parties might well have contemplated that at the end of the period of separation one or other would seek a divorce. Under the wording of this bill would it not then be the duty of the court to refuse to grant divorce on the ground that the petition was based on the consent of the parties?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Taking the example he has given, would not the consent be consent to the separation, not consent to the divorce? In other words, the court would be passing judgment not on the consent to separate but on the issue of divorce.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I confess the wording is ambiguous. It says the court should refuse a divorce based on consent. If the court found that the consent of the parties was the basis of the divorce proceedings it might well interpret the bill as saying that divorce should be refused, and this would negative the provision for divorce based on separation. I suggest to the minister that before we get to committee this point be looked at again in order that the sense of it may be clarified, because the reality of the matter is that many divorces are and always will be based upon consent, whatever subterfuges may be forced on the parties to conceal the element of consent.
[DOT] (12 noon)
I agree with many hon. members who have the view that divorce should not be based solely on consent. The marriage contract is not a mere private contract of partnership that can be terminated at the will of the parties. Marriage creates obligations with which the state is concerned. It is important

that there be independent tribunals so that people cannot unilaterally, or even by agreement, get out of the obligations created by marriage. I am not suggesting that agreement by itself should be sufficient to bring about a divorce, but it is quite unrealistic to say that because the parties happen to agree they should not have a divorce. Under existing law, as a lot of people know, many divorces are arranged, but it is nevertheless necessary for the parties to go through a parade of empty words before the courts. They are obliged to swear on oath that in fact there is no element of agreement or consent although this is often not true.
It is in this context that I want to deal with the provisions of the bill with respect to reconciliation. I suggest they will be virtually useless. Clause 7 provides that the legal adviser should draw attention to the provisions of the legislation with regard to reconciliation. Clause 8 provides that the court may adjourn a hearing for divorce in order to afford an opportunity for marriage reconciliation or marriage counselling. Judging by the experience in divorce courts today, the total effect of this is likely to be the addition of some extra words to the formal pleadings, plus the addition of a few extra sentences at the trial. Counsel or the judge will ask a few perfunctory questions about attempts at reconciliation. This is particularly true where the divorce is based upon the old grounds of adultery and matrimonial misconduct. Now lawyers will have to add another formula to the three c's they have been asking about in the past.
However, I point out that if the breakdown principle were adopted it would alter the existing situation. In that case it would give substance to the question of reconciliation. A judge would not make, except in the case of a long separation, a finding of complete breakdown of the marriage until satisfied that a reasonable attempt at reconciliation had been made. This would make it a matter of substance rather than a mere matter of formality.
If I may sum up on this aspect of the bill before us, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that it is really a continuation, with changes, of the old system. It rejects a new approach. It seems to me to be quite ridiculous for the government to say, as many members supporting it have said, that public opinion is not ready to accept such a sweeping change in the law and that we must maintain the old, familiar concepts. The fact of the matter is that the churches, usually noted for a
December 15, 1967

conservative approach to questions of marriage, have opted for the new approach and have urged it upon the government.
The churches are naturally conservative in matters of this sort. Although they have disclaimed any intention of forcing their opinions upon others who do not share their faith, they are particularly concerned about the stability of the family and marriage as a permanent institution. But the churches have been able to say, and nearly all of them have said, that when a marriage has broken down and there is no hope of reconciliation the institution of marriage is more honoured by declaring that it is at an end than it is in trying to maintain empty legal ties. In these circumstances I find it strange to hear a Liberal government, and a Liberal party that prides itself on being a party of reform, maintain that the churches have gone too far and are too radical and that public opinion will not accept such a change. It is not just the churches which have urged the new approach. Social workers, experts in mental health, councils of women and some of the most experienced lawyers have also given their support to the new approach.
Now that the government has accepted the other, more old-fashioned approach, the approach adopted in Britain more than 30 years ago, and has declared this bill to be a government measure, I suppose there is little likelihood of a quick change of mind and we shall once again have to accept the second best. However, I hope that this discussion and the issues involved will be the subject of widespread examination by the Canadian people, and that it will not be too long before the legislators as well as the people are ready for a totally new approach to the question.
There is one other general matter, although it is partly a matter of detail, of great importance in regard to the bill that I wish to raise. I refer to the decision of the minister and the government to turn down the unanimous recommendation of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons that jurisdiction in respect of divorce in provinces other than Quebec and Newfoundland should be conferred upon county and district courts and not confined to supreme courts.
The committee heard a strong plea in this regard from former Chief Justice McRuer of the Supreme Court of Ontario. He pointed out that judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario-and I think the same is true in other provinces-go on circuit throughout the
Divorce Law Reform
province. They may visit a particular county town once in five years or ten years or only once. Therefore the judges of the Supreme Court are not accessible in large parts of the country. Yet this bill gives jurisdiction to that court with regard to all sorts of ancillary and corollary provisions dealing with maintenance and custody, provisions that have been varied from time to time and which require constant supervision. The minister has said that the matters involved in divorce are at least of equal importance to property matters dealt with by the highest courts. Of course they are as important, perhaps more important, but intimate family affairs are better dealt with by a court closer to the people and more accessible to the people.
Another advantage of transferring jurisdiction to the county courts or district courts would be that it would substantially cut down the cost of divorces. This is surely an extremely important matter. I wonder why the decision of the committee, which was composed of many lawyers from all parts of Canada serving both in the Senate and the House of Commons, was turned down. I can only suspect that someone with a more academic acquaintance with the subject decided that the matter should be confined to the supreme courts alone. I urge the minister to reconsider this point.

Divorce Law Reform

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, in 1967, we are discussing the proposed reform of a law we inherited in 1867 that was based on the English law of 1867, which law was completely altered in 1937, and is more antiquated than the law of Rome in 37 B.C. The world of our great-great-grandfathers was a completely different world from our world in this centennial year. Yet most of our social laws have hardly changed. No laws in Canada are crying out more for reform than our divorce laws. They cause more suffering than did the rack in the middle ages.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
It would be an ideal world if every married couple lived happily ever after. For various reasons marriages go on the rocks, families break up. The reasons are legion. It may simply be because the wrong people went to the altar. It may be because of the immaturity of the partners, a failure to adjust, lack of understanding of the responsibilities of marriage, or even simple selfishness on the part of one partner or both. I have personally seen dozens of situations where because of one mistake people have been condemned to unhappiness and frustrating loneliness owing to our antiquated and uncivilized divorce laws.
For example, I recall the case of a girl who married at the age of 18. Three months later her husband deserted her. A child was born seven months after the desertion. Since that time the husband has travelled all over North America. She has attempted almost frantically to obtain evidence of adultery on his part. She has been unable to afford the tremendous detective fees and 15 years later is still trying to find evidence of adultery. During this period of 15 years she has supported herself and her daughter. The daughter is now a lovely teenager going to high school. For the past ten years this woman has wished to remarry. She refuses to live with the man with whom she is in love because of her child and her own religious views. Here is a girl who has excellent marital prospects but because of a youthful mistake is confined to a form of imprisonment from which there is at present no escape.
Many people, of course, do not have the self-discipline and views of the lady I just mentioned. Personally I know of hundreds of so-called common law relationships. In most cases illegitimate children are born and in many cases the couple live together as happily as possible. However, they live together

under tension created by the fear that their neighbours, friends and fellow workers may find out. When the children start to school the names on the birth certificates create crises. The sense of guilt, the recurrent feelings of insecurity, are always just below the surface. Unhappiness is not only promoted; immorality and illegitimacy are invited.
One of the strongest indictments against our present divorce law is the fact that disrespect for the law is the natural result. This disrespect amplifies into a disrespect for all laws. Seldom is adultery the real cause of a marriage breakup. In order to obtain a divorce adultery must be found or created. My experience in hundreds of these cases has convinced me that in only a very small percentage is there not perjury or collusion. I have observed almost a contempt for the law in the minds of the people involved. This is a most natural human reaction, because how can a law be respected when a single act of adultery is considered far worse than 20 years of beatings or far worse than a man deserting his family or going to jail for 20 years? On no rational or religious grounds can such laws be defended.
May I say a few words about the marriage breakdown concept. There is no doubt whatsoever in my mind that when a marriage has irretrievably broken down it should be dissolved if one of the parties desires dissolution. This would not be a case of breaking up a marriage; it would simply be a case of making legal what has in fact already happened. To confine ourselves to the principle of matrimonial offence is to give no relief to either party when a man and wife without misconduct or matrimonial offence, have become so estranged as to be beyond the possibility of reconciliation. It would give no relief either when the so-called innocent party refuses to take the initiative and seek a dissolution, preferring to imprison the other party within bonds which become meaningless.
The elimination of the marriage offence provision and substitution of the breakdown theory would result in something which would be difficult to carry out in practice. The law must have definite rules; otherwise the people affected will not know where they stand and the lawyers who advise them will not be in a position to give definite advice.
In the past few months I have attempted to give the problem very serious thought in the light of my own practical experience and particularly in the light of the experience of
December 15, 1967

others who have been closely connected with the practical problems. I have concluded that the proposed bill is excellent and that the retention of the matrimonial offence theory, plus the introduction of the marriage breakdown theory, is by far the most realistic and practical approach.
If divorce were to be granted solely as a result of the breakdown of the marriage, the result could well be long delay in determining whether the marriage actually had broken down even though the situation was crying out for a remedy. The fact is that the vast majority of problems will be solved under the matrimonial offences provision. Those that will not be solved under this provision will be solved under the recognition of marriage breakdown, proven by three years of separation and subject to the discretion of the court. I have observed over the years that once a couple has actually separated for a considerable period of time the chances of reconciliation are very slight. When one party has indicated a desire for divorce and has commenced proceedings the chances of reconciliation have been reduced to almost nil.
I am pleased to note the presence of clauses 7 and 8 which relate to marriage counselling and reconciliation. In considering the whole question of marriage and divorce our prime objective to promote marriage and to protect the family must be maintained. When a marriage has deteriorated to the point where one of the parties is actively considering the dissolution of the marriage bond, the likelihood is that the marriage has deteriorated beyond repair. The marriage then has gone beyond the point of no return.
We agree that the time for counselling and the educational process is before the first cracks in the marriage begin to occur. This period is both before marriage and early in marriage. Sometimes we do not appreciate the adjustment required by marriage. Two persons who had no need whatsoever to consider the interest of anyone but themselves suddenly must adjust and accommodate each other. This adjustment carries on throughout life and marriage as people change.
As soon as possible we should make provision for counselling. This should be patterned on the provision introduced in Australia in 1961. Australia's matrimonial causes act provides for support to marriage guidance organizations. As I understand the act, provision is made for both voluntary and full time counselling services for both premarital education and marital counselling. A complete
Divorce Law Reform
program and network must be set up. The availability of this program must be known generally. The reluctance to seek help must be overcome. There must be no shame or stigma attached when both parties actively and sincerely seek assistance. Many marriages which would otherwise be broken can be made viable and happy if help is given early enough.
The bill, unfortunately, does not follow the recommendation of the committee with respect to giving jurisdiction to the county courts. Like the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) I am in favour of giving the county courts concurrent jurisdiction with the supreme courts in the matter of divorce. In Ontario actions for divorce have taken their place in a long list of cases to be tried as rapidly as possible in a short time. If there are recurrent problems it is impossible in most cases to arrange to have the matters brought before the same judge who heard the case in the first instance. In the county courts, on the other hand, the judges are local. Appointments can readily be made and orders with respect to children and maintenance can be explained or reconsidered with the minimum of procedure. By this means costs could be greatly reduced. Of course, when we reform our divorce laws the divorce rate will increase. For a time, of course, the number of cases will increase greatly because of the great backlog of broken marriages in respect of which relief has been denied. After this accumulation has been taken care of the rate will still be higher than previously. This need not alarm us, however. The increase will simply reflect the reduction in common law marriages.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
I disagree with the view that an increase in the divorce rate indicates a weakening of the institution of marriage. On the contrary, the fact that a person seeks a divorce to bring to an end a shell of a marriage is an indication of greater respect for the institution of marriage. It is the widespread common law marriages with their illegitimate children that seriously threaten the institution of marriage. The great reduction in the indicence of these relationships that will follow the enactment of this bill will strengthen and foster both marriage and the family.
We in Canada had a great ability to retain our Victorianism in the twentieth century. While England, Australia, New Zealand, Scotland and other commonwealth and European countries have reformed their divorce

December 15, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
laws to reflect modern conditions and views, we have lagged behind. We have not only lacked the courage to innovate, we have lacked the courage to follow. We have condemned tens of thousands of our people to unhappiness and immorality. While thinking we are perserving the family we are in actual fact undermining the family. Let us make this a real centennial year for all those we have imprisoned through our archaic laws by passing this bill.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Stafford) in spite of the fact that he and I part company on one aspect of the problem which faces us. I suggest to him that if he will read his speech in Hansard tomorrow he will see that the arguments he has made in fact buttress, support and lend foundation to the belief which I hold and which has been expressed by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and other members on this side, that irretrievable marriage breakdown with certain safeguards can be the only ground upon which a marriage can be dissolved. It is my belief after listening to the hon. member that his arguments point in that one direction.
In any event, legislation of this kind touches closely and deeply the social conscience of all of us, as it must. I think that when we come to methods we must weigh any legislation on the scales of balance of the good of society. We must decide what are the good points and what are the bad. We must place on the scales the different views we hold and the different points we advance to find out whether on balance the good features of this legislation outweigh the bad. With great reluctance I must say I will vote for this bill on second reading because there is certain specific good it will do, but I must also say that there are many aspects which I think it is a great pity the government has seen fit to introduce in the legislation in the face of what I believe is an irresistible movement toward accepting the marriage breakdown philosophy as being the sole ground for dissolution. In my judgment, and I venture to make a prediction, within ten years most of the countries which have now dealt with the problem of divorce will have embraced the philosophy of marriage breakdown as the sole ground for divorce.
What are the good points? The very fact that there is a change and that this legislation breaks loose the solid grip in which this country has been held for so many years in

regard to the very serious and difficult social problem of divorce is good. The minister, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Stafford), and others have said that the subject of divorce takes us back to the first divorce bill in the United Kingdom around 1857 which, as a matter of fact, was simply a restating of old ecclesiastical law developed over many centuries. It provided that adultery would be the ground, not for the dissolution of marriage, and I hasten to point that out, but for divorce from bed and board. The only exception to that was, I think, shortly after the accession of King Henry VIII to the throne and his becoming head of the church. He, being somewhat of a marrying man, came to the conclusion that he either had to cut off his respective wives' heads or divorce them. He decided that it was probably less expensive to cut off their heads than to go through the process of divorce.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: We have made some progress.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Outside of that exception in Great Britain, in ecclesiastical law adultery was the ground not for dissolution of marriage but for separation from bed and board. Late in 1857 this was brought up to date and allowed for the dissolution of the mariage in the United Kingdom and so became the law in Canada. It has subsisted here for some 100 years. Now we are at least making a change. We are breaking out of the grip in which these ancient laws have held us.
Another provision has been introduced in the bill which I have no hesitation in saying is an improvement, and I refer to the provisions in respect of domicile. Many members of the bar who have struggled with the very difficult problem of domicile in the ten provinces are very glad, I am sure, to see that the recommendation of the joint committee has been virtually adopted so that there may be Canadian domicile. This will do away with the double standard and put married women, to all intents and purposes, in the same position as their husbands. I congratulate the minister and the government on this very excellent change which is so very desirable.
With regard to the introduction for the first time into the courts dealing with matrimonial issues of these provisions for certain conciliation procedures, I think they are fumbling and weak and that a great deal of difficulty will be experienced in trying to apply them. But at least this is a beginning. This is not an easy problem because of the
December 15. 1967



lack ol precedents. It is only recently that in Australia and New Zealand, and I believe in the United Kingdom, a somewhat similar proposal has been the subject of serious consideration. Society must regard the institution of marriage as its most important unit. Society must be concerned, as well as the individuals who are involved, with making every effort to preserve marriage and to preserve couples in the bonds of matrimony for the sake of society, for the sake of the children and for the sake of everything else that is involved.
The other day I spoke on this subject to a club in Calgary. A meeting had been held, sponsored by the university there, at which some professor had made a speech. The next day in the newspaper headlines appeared to the effect that this professor had suggested that the cure for divorce is trial marriage. This is a very interesting suggestion but it seems to me it involves one of the difficulties we face today. Many television programs and books relating to the disintegration of the bonds of family units make the suggestion that there can be a complete abandonment of those things that have been held sacred and upon which western civilization as we know it has been fashioned and improved. This is a very dangerous suggestion and I welcome any attempt, no matter what its faults may be and no matter what defects we may see in it, on the part of the government to recognize the role of the courts and government services to try to preserve marriage and to link this attempt with the new divorce procedure. I think any such recognition is excellent and represents a step forward. My guess is that within five or ten years so many changes will be made in these procedures that the minister will not recognize them.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
I should now like to state very briefly my criticism of this aspect. I think there will be a tendency for an automatic approach to the procedure in regard to conciliation. Lawyers consulted by a litigant seeking a divorce will now be compelled to give certain advice to their clients and they must endorse this fact upon the pleadings. The court is directed to give the respondent, if he or she is available, as well as the petitioner notice that these conciliation procedures are available. I think it will become automatic in the same sense as today there are automatic questions and answers with regard to condonation and collusion. However, this provision is a start and
Divorce Law Reform
to that extent I am very happy to see it in the bill.
I am also pleased to see that at long last we have done away with that travesty of the legislative process by which parliament was required to sit as a judge and deal with private bills for the relief of people seeking divorce. For too long this has been a black mark on the record of parliament. I am very happy to note that the procedures contained in the bill will provide, first, for a divorce division of the exchequer court and ultimately, I hope, the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland will see fit to clothe their courts with jurisdiction to dissolve marriages by the method provided in the bill.
I am also very very glad to see that the opinion given by Mr. Driedger, then deputy minister of justice, to the committee to the effect that in his opinion-I should say that he hedged it with the statement that he was giving it not necessarily as deputy minister but as his personal legal opinion-the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction to deal with ancillary and related matters of custody of children, maintenance and alimony. In fact, I think Mr. Driedger went as far as to suggest that this jurisdiction would include dealing with judicial separation.
This is something to which we may have to come in due course. I recognize that various provincial legislatures have dealt with this question. It is a subject that has not been dealt with by a federal government. I doubt that a case dealing implicitly with this question and which has established a binding precedent has been dealt with by the supreme court. I am glad to see that parliament will now recognize this question so that we will ultimately have a situation where one court alone can deal with all the issues which are so closely and intimately related to marriage and its dissolution.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, another good feature of this measure is that at long last there will be an opportunity for the thousands of people all over this country, who have for so many years been handicapped because of the grim rigidity of our divorce law, to legitimize the unions which so many of them have in good faith and with the best intentions in the world entered into. I think all of us know people who because of the reluctance of the other party, religious scruples or various other reasons have not had a legal dissolution of their marriages, and one party has then entered into an illegal liaison with somebody else and children have been born of that

December 15, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
union. In some cases these unions have subsisted since the first world war. I believe that this bill, through its provision dealing with marriage breakdown will bring relief, help and assistance to the thousands of people who have waited so long for such a measure to be introduced.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I have exhausted all the good things I can say about the bill. I must say that I thoroughly agree with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) who said it was unfortunate that the government and the minister had not seen fit to adopt the principle of marriage breakdown. In respect of that aspect of the bill which attempts to bring together these obviously opposing views, I can only say that in my opinion it is a ramshackle, motley conglomeration of inconsistent and irreconcilable proposals which will never work. It is my belief that within a few years whatever government is in power will be asking parliament to enact necessary and essential modifications to the law in this respect.
This bill continues the principle of matrimonial offence whereby one person must be the offender and the other must be innocent. One is black, one is white; one is guilty of a matrimonial offence, the other is innocent. This raises the whole question of the consideration of matrimonial offences and the dissolution of marriage. In my view this position is not sound and does not correspond to facts.
I recall sitting in a court waiting for a case in which I was concerned to be tried. I listened to a supreme court judge complete the hearing of ten cases and grant decree nisis in one hour. That is six minutes a case. How is it possible for a judge in five or six minutes to go through the formal proof of the marriage, the formal proof of domicile, the formal proof that there was no condonation and no collusion? How is it possible for a judge, devoting approximately two minutes to each of these points, to say that because of an allegation of adultery which has been proved by evidence of a certain type a dissolution of marriage shall be granted? How can he in six minutes undo 20 years of marriage and conjugal life? I think those of us who have been concerned professionally in the practice of law will agree that the practice to which I have just referred is not sound. I believe this fact is being increasingly recognized in many countries throughout the world.
I have here the Montreal Star of Friday, November 24 which contains an article on

the proposed new divorce law in the United Kingdom. I notice that the measure has not been introduced by the government, although the government has indicated that it will give tacit approval to the bill which will be introduced by a private member. I shall deal with this matter later. I do not know whether the minister has been able to secure a copy of the bill which has been introduced in that country. All I have in the newspaper article is a condensed report of the major provisions of the bill. England has experimented with its divorce law, as I believe the hon. member for Elgin and the hon. member for Greenwood said, since 1937 as a result of the book "Holy Deadlock", written by Sir Alan Herbert. The government widened the grounds for divorce and has now had 30 years of experience with those wider grounds based upon matrimonial offences. All those who are concerned with this question, sociologists, judges, people in public life, the clergy, all those who direct their attention to this problem, are satisfied beyond any reasonable doubt that the principle of the matrimonial offence must be eliminated. The following is proposed in the new bill introduced in the United Kingdom:
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
There will henceforth be only one ground for divorce in Britain-proof that "the marriage has irretrievably broken down". This will be deemed to have happened:
(a)	If the parties have ceased to cohabit for two years...
(b)	If the couple have ceased to cohabit for five years, even though one does not want divorce ...
(c)	If there is conduct which a husband or wife cannot be reasonably expected to endure, or adultery which either cannot after reflection forgive.
However, even these provisions do not go as far as I would like them to go. I should like to see the addition of a provision stating "and for such other reasons as may seem adequate to the court". In other words, a catch-all phrase would be inserted which would entitle a court to say that the marriage has irretrievably broken down for other reasons related to but not necessarily the same as those which have already been set down.
I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood that in fact the government is only paying lip service to the marriage breakdown philosophy. I think it is merely attempting to appease a very substantial body of public opinion represented by various church groups and womens organizations as well as other people who have felt that the marriage breakdown philosophy should be adopted in
December 15, 1967

the new legislation, and that in using the words "marriage breakdown" there may be a hope on the part of the government, if not on the part of the minister, that this will appease and satisfy them. We are still harking back to the virtually mediaeval conditions under which there was trial by ordeal and under which if a man had been injured or killed through accident by an inanimate object the court would try that inanimate object and find it guilty. Sometimes a man accused of a criminal offence would have his arms and legs tied and would be thrown into a pool of water. If he rose to the top he was deemed to be guilty and was immediately taken out and executed, but if he did not rise he was deemed innocent. However, all too often, even when the accused was finally brought up from the bottom he was drowned in any event and it did not matter.
I do not know how carefully the matter of divorce was studied and I do not know to what extent the government seriously considered adopting the marriage breakdown philosophy, but I must say I am bitterly disappointed with what they have done. Let us take a look at the bill and see to what extent it substantiates my view. A draft bill was attached to the report of the joint committee. It provided for certain matrimonial offences and in subsequent sections it went on to provide that certain acts should also be considered as constructively establishing marriage breakdown.
Under the bill before us anyone seeking a divorce will first direct his or her attention to clause 3 which provides four grounds as the basis for dissolution of marriage, namely, adultery, acts of sodomy, bestiality, rape or homosexuality, most of which have already been considered and accepted by the courts as being a basis for the dissolution of marriage. Another ground for divorce is when a person has gone through a form of marriage with another person. This is in fact adultery because anyone going through a form of marriage with a person other than his or her spouse must have the intention of going to bed with that person shortly after the marriage, which is in effect constructive adultery. The final ground for divorce is when a person has treated the petitioner with physical or mental cruelty of such a kind as to render intolerable the continued cohabitation of the spouses.
What will happen is that people seeking a divorce will first turn their attention to the provisions of clause 3 in looking for a quick divorce or a "quickie", as it has been called
Divorce Law Reform
in some speeches. Under clause 3 there will be an opportunity for an immediate petition to be issued claiming the dissolution of marriage on the ground of either adultery or cruelty. For those who are adverse to committing adultery for the purpose of securing a quick divorce or in cases where cruelty cannot be established, clause 4 will provide an answer. It contains all that can be considered in this bill as coming within the four corners of the marriage breakdown philosophy. It provides an alternative means of securing a divorce when it cannot be secured on the ground of adultery or cruelty, namely, minor or inferior matrimonial offences or constructive marriage breakdown established by certain specific acts.
All the witnesses and organizations which appeared before the joint committee and proposed the adoption of the marriage breakdown philosophy stated quite clearly that in their opinion these two differing philosophies cannot be included together. Let me refer to the evidence of Reverend Hosking, a very distinguished member of the clergy who has also had experience in the family courts. He was a very impressive witness. When asked whether it is possible to have these two opposing principles in one bill he said:
I am sitting here as a witness, but I would hope to high heaven you would not do that, for this reason. This is something fundamental: You are lifting the struggle from the shoulders of husband and wife and looking at the institution known as marriage in a way that removes from it much of the bitterness and sense of failure and hopeless frustration. For heaven's sake, let us take our courage in our two fists and make this step. For I think it is profoundly sound; and, speaking as a religious person, I believe it is the will of God. I honestly do.
This is the view taken by all those who have considered this new approach. All of them have come to the firm decision that it is not possible to link these two principles or these two means of securing a dissolution of marriage. This is amply established by the fact that in England they have come to the same conclusion, having pioneered much of the new forward looking legislation dealing with the problem of divorce. In their view marriage breakdown is the only basis for a divorce. I should like to refer to the article from which I quoted previously in which Mr. Abse, a member of the British parliament who has been keenly interested in this issue, is reported as arguing that the aim of the bill

December 15, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
is not easier divorce but rational divorce. He said:
I am for the family, not against it. A divorce is the death certificate of a dead marriage. You can't stop people dying by refusing to issue death certificates.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
I think I have made it quite clear where I stand on this issue. I just want to refer to one or two of the objections which have been raised to the marriage breakdown theory. It has been suggested that marriage breakdown is not a triable issue. I think this is nonsense. The minister took it a step further in his speech on second reading and said it would appear too much like an inquisition rather than a trial. The minute the government introduced the conciliation procedure they introduce a peg upon which there will from time to time be hung in process of an inquisition. Trials in all courts involve the process of inquisition. I do not think that is a fair answer at all.
However, the suggestion it is not a triable issue is, I think, one which must be met. I should like to look at some of the problems which courts have met, very much more difficult problems than having to make a declaration that a marriage which has irretrievably broken down, in which there is no hope of reconciliation, is dead and ought to be so legally pronounced. The courts have tackled successfully the defence of insanity, the burden of proof in criminal cases, that is, establishing guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The courts have had a mandate from parliament to deal with problems under the Restrictive Trade Practices Act and the Combines Investigation Act which involve a difficult assessment of the result of present actions.
I think there is no real problem at all in this regard. When two people find they are unable to live together, that marriage, something which was once alive, is then dead. There are only the ashes left and no fire can be breathed into those ashes. The marriage should be dissolved. There may be difficulty for the courts, but the courts exist to serve the people. The minister might look at it in this way, that specific directions could be given to the courts which would permit them to evolve a jurisprudence over a period of time by which it would be, if not easy, at least possible for the courts to declare there had been a breakdown of the marriage.
As a matter of fact, I think there is some recognition of that principle in the bill. The draft bill proposed by the committee, which

appears on page 159 of the report of the committee, provided that two of the grounds which would be established as matrimonial offences were desertion for a period of three years and wilful refusal to consummate the marriage for a period of at least one year. When we come to the constructive grounds which the government has introduced in clause 4 of the bill as being the basis for marriage breakdown, we find they have lifted these two proposals out of the section which provided for the creation of matrimonial offences. The minister has said, we will not accept these as matrimonial offences but we will accept them as constituting a basis upon which a court can deem the marriage has broken down. This is proof of the proposition I have been trying to make that the line between matrimonial offences and marriage breakdown is very tenous and should no longer be continued.
I suggest this quite seriously, Mr. Speaker. I know that at this time the government has all the pride of paternity in this legislation. The minister has indicated, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has confirmed, that there will not be a free vote on this issue. There is no doubt that this bill, with some improvements and modifications, is going to pass. I sincerely hope that, after it passes, what has been said in this house and what has been said in all the briefs that have been presented to the committee will be given the most earnest and serious consideration. I hope the government will not be wedded to these proposals in the bill, at least not to the extent that the old marriage and divorce legislation which we have had in this country has been continued in the past. I hope that in the course of his reply the minister will give an indication that the principle of marriage breakdown as the sole cause will not be abandoned. Perhaps in the light of the experience of the courts there will be another look at this matter within two or three years.
The only other point I want to make is to confirm what has been said by the hon. member for Elgin and the hon. member for Greenwood. Why should not county and district courts be given jurisdiction? The minister has said that divorce is a very important and fundamental matter, but so is 20 years in prison. The district and county courts have jurisdiction to impose substantial sentences in criminal cases. As a matter of fact, I think it is about time we took a look at the division of jurisdiction between county and superior
December 15, 1967

courts. I do not know why we should have on one side of the street 5 and 10 cent store justice merely because the judge receives a lower salary and on the other side of the road have plush department store justice for the carriage trade, and yet this is implicit in what is said. I think it is about time we eliminated all these distinctions.
The courts are going to be engaged in a great many trials of divorce issues which will follow the completion of this bill. Surely the government should be prepared to allow county and district courts to try these issues to ease the load which will have to be carried. I hope before we get into committee the minister will give some indication of his interest in this matter. I hope he is not hidebound and is prepared to consider the proposal made by members of his own party as well as members of this party to invest county and district courts with the power to hear these trials for the dissolution of marriage.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Registrar General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I deem it advisable to take part in the debate on this bill because to my mind very serious implications are involved for our society as we have known it up to now. I wanted also to bring to the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) some suggestions which, I am sure, must have been considered, just as the other factors that have been brought to his attention, concerning the bill now before us which provides for a reform in depth of our divorce laws.
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with considerable attention to the comments of the preceding speakers, particularly those of the member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). However, I must say that even though I sat on the divorce committee, most of my time was taken up by the finance, trade and economic affairs committee sitting concurrently. Nevertheless, this did not prevent me from reading most attentively all the briefs presented.
Divorce Law Reform
I should like at this stage to make some observations on the remarks of the hon. member for Greenwood concerning what is commonly called marriage breakdown.
Mr. Speaker, in considering the clauses of the proposed bill, more specifically clauses 3 and 4, we realize that on the whole the government is being blamed for not going far enough with this measure. As I reject marriage breakdown as the essential and only valid ground for divorce, I should like to bring forward an opinion or at least a thought.
I have read with considerable attention the briefs that were presented by some religious authorities on this point. To my mind, what is difficult to reconcile is the permanent marriage breakdown with clause 4 of the bill. In fact, if marriage breakdown were accepted as grounds for divorce, I think we should conclude that this would overly facilitate or at least considerably facilitate in the mind of husband and wife the possibilities of obtaining a divorce.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Even though the briefs submitted to the committee were to the effect that marriage breakdown could not be agreed upon by mutual consent, I fail to see how one could possibly suggest, by the same token, that marriage breakdown does not enable to obtain a divorce by mutual consent, a solution that the bill is trying to prevent.
Mr. Speaker, it is precisely on that particular point that the bill, even though some may feel it does not go far enough, gives rises, both in its spirit and its letter, to the serious thought that a state cannot possibly admit that a married couple can, merely by mutual consent, without giving any reason or justification, obtain a divorce, which would be possible, if the principle of marriage breakdown were accepted as criterion.
But when the champions of that theory tell us that this does not allow divorce by mutual consent, but merely becomes a permanent breakdown in the marriage, I refer them to clause 4 of the bill which, to my mind, gives wise and intelligent support to those who claim that a permanent breakdown of the marriage is sufficient cause for divorce. We see that in particular in clause 4 of the bill and more specifically in paragraphs (b), (c), (d) and (e) where it is stipulated that a spouse may petition for divorce when the respondent has been grossly addicted to alcohol for three years, or has deserted him

December 15, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
for the same period, or after a year where the marriage has not been consummated, and where, in fact, the spouses have lived separately for over three years, or where one has abandoned the other for five years.
What is it, if it is not, really and truly, marriage breakdown? However, there may have been a degree of shock about clause 3; perhaps the legal profession did come to the conclusion that it is generally disagreeable, for the parents as well as the children, to have to publicize the grounds for their separation, or again, before a divorce is granted, to have to commit acts of cruelty or others.
Mr. Speaker, I think the bill as it now stands is based on a sound principle, which is to respect the marriage institution and that the state should try as much as possible to consolidate it. The acceptance of the marriage breakdown concept as the only grounds for divorce is a confirmation by the state that a married couple may, by mutual consent, agree to separate for a period of one, two or three years, and then, without any other factor than such a separation, be able to secure a divorce.
Of course, my hon. friend from Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) will object that this is perhaps not possible in practice, but this makes it too easy to get a divorce. And when the state takes it for granted or wants to maintain the de facto responsibility for both husband and wife in important cases, the crown will be forcing the spouses or those about to be married to understand that it is a contract or a compromise and that, in such a case, there must be tolerance, forbearance and sound understanding, above all because it gives crucial importance to the sad and deplorable results for society and unfortunately a cause for divorce occurs, especially if there are children from such marriages that are terminated by decree.

A wife may demand the separation on the ground of her husband's adultery when he keeps his mistress in their own home.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to most speeches delivered on divorce. I should like to point out three that I found particularly interesting, that of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), and the one of hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Laflamme).
From another point of view I find the presentation of this bill rather amusing. I
Divorce Law Reform
wish to point out that it took a Minister of Justice who is a confirmed bachelor to present a bill so up to date on the question of marriage. I hope this will not convince the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) to remain unmarried until the end of his days, because, after all, the country should not be deprived of such brilliant offsprings, since the potential father is so much so. I would not want him either to be discouraged from taking a wife, because of all the disquieting things he has been hearing in this house.
Mr. Speaker, all this to say in a rather light vein, that it was high time for the divorce legislation to be improved.
I shall not discuss it from a legal point of view, because I am not qualified to do so, nor from a moral point of view, because it seems to me that is not our concern. I think we all agree, here in the house, that divorce in itself is an evil. As far as I am concerned, my religion tells me it is inadmissible. The fact remains, however, that we also believe, and more strongly than ever since the last council held by the authorities of my Church, where oecumenism and similar topics were discussed, that it is not admissible either that we, legislators, Catholics or others, should impose our convictions on those Canadians who do not share our convictions.
Mr. Speaker, like most hon. members in this house, I believe, for instance, that human life is sacred. However, I recognize that, under certain circumstances, such as war, self-defence and, as I persist in believing, retribution, the state has the right to take human lives, to put people to death.
Personally, I feel that the physical integrity of a human being, man or woman, is also sacred, but, in some cases, to prevent a greater evil, an arm or a leg may be amputated, an organ may be removed.
So, I think we should consider the matter of divorce somewhat in the same light. In itself, it is wrong; morally speaking, my conscience tells me it should not be allowed; still, there may be borderline cases, people who hold divergent views, and we have no right to impose upon them such conditions as would lead them to live immoral or hypocritical lives.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
That is why I find it comforting that the Canadian spokesmen for religious groups of every hue should have told us that it was high time to amend the divorce legislation, even to modernize it, and put an end to the

hypocrisy which leads to perjury and false representations. There is no need to dwell on the subject for it was taken up brilliantly in this house, and I am quite convinced that all the members of this house even if the bill is not perfect, must approve of it in principle. We shall never have a perfect bill in this house, although we may have bills that are less imperfect. The fact remains that this bill certainly has its good points, that it improves the situation even if every member can still suggest amendments.
Still Mr. Speaker, some figures are shocking and we simply cannot refuse to take notice. For instance, there were in Canada, at the close of 1966, about 400,000 people-this figure comes from authoritative social agencies-living in common law marriage. So, we may reasonably assume that many of these people, if more reasonable divorce legislation had been available, would not live that way and would probably be living in more normal conditions.
At the end of 1961, there were in Canada
81.000	separated women living alone, in many cases in conditions of hardship, and of this number 15,600 were divorced. I am speaking only about women, but we can assume that the same figures probably apply to men.
In the United States, in 1965, there were
1.780.000	marriages, and of these 481,000 broke up within one year or since and most recent statistics show that there are 6 million divorced people in the United States.
Naturally, this is not a situation of which most of my colleagues and I can approve in conscience, but it is a definite situation which must be faced and which we cannot refuse to examine in order to see whether it could not be helped in some way.
I wonder, therefore, whether we might not look at this divorce law in a broader context, and whether we should not add to it a preventive measure against divorce, so as to create a certain cohesion between all the social welfare agencies and family services in the country. In doing this, we could first reduce the causes of divorce and then try to act as mediators, negotiators or advisers, when trouble starts in a marriage, to prevent that final rupture between two people called divorce, which is always regrettable.
Aside from the religious considerations of which I spoke earlier, there are natural considerations which make divorce normally unacceptable. One of the best studies of this problem, or at least that which seems to me

to be the best, was written by representatives of various religious denominations and submitted to parliament by the Canadian Anglican Church, through its Christian Social Service. I am translating as best I can, for I only have the English text.

In my opinion, this study-and we have received a great deal of documentation-is excellent.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I may quote some passages from it at this stage of our consideration of the divorce bill, because I think it expresses my opinion better than I could express it myself.
This brief says, and I quote;
In this collective brief, however, we feel that there is presently in Canada a common agreement on the need for reform of our legislation in order to facilitate the setting up of more adequate social welfare facilities to settle marital troubles.
And this should be emphasized, Mr. Speaker, that as legislators we would fail in our responsibilities if we merely make divorce easier in the case of marriage breakdown. I think we should add, parallel to this legislation, some provision making it possible to prevent marital trouble and cure it when it has become too serious.
And the brief goes on to say:

I will quote a few cases which have come to my knowledge since the last few weeks. I have in mind, for instance, a particularly sad case where, for 7 or 8 years, every effort was

made, with the help of matrimonial agencies, to make the marriage successful, but, as things now stand, there is no solution possible, other than a legal separation. This, not a divorce, has been requested.
The poor wife who must ask for a judicial separation is told by her lawyer: you have to deposit $300. She does not have it, Mr. Speaker. In that case, will she have to bear her lot till the end of her days? Would not legal aid have a formula or could not the state provide that inherent expenses be reduced in keeping with the means of those who may require divorce or judicial separation? Otherwise, people will continue to say that there is a double standard of justice in our country: one for the poor and another for the rich. I think a situation where such things can still be said is unwholesome.
I continue reading the brief:
(2)	Divorce proceedings are taken as a last resort in the case of a marriage which, obviously, seems to have broken down. The ideal is to ensure a lasting marriage-
-in that respect, everyone agrees-
-and that ideal will be achieved only if the preparation starts at home and continues through educational programs sponsored by schools or other organizations. Those organizations should receive public funds as a help and as an encouragement to private enterprise.
There, of course, I see the need for a conference in the future between the provinces and the federal government to discuss legislation, to reconcile the laws which might be urgent, for instance, in the case of Quebec and Canada, to undertake that educational program, to prevent marriage from floundering on the shoals of misunderstanding or other reasons.
Here is another extract of the report:
(3)	Sometimes, even the best of marriages may be in need of counselling at a given moment. All Canadians should be able to have access to such services. And in order for these services to be effective, it is necessary for the state to have an interest in them and to help them financially.
Some already exist. Perhaps there is a lack of co-ordination throughout the country. Perhaps they lack the means of improving techniques by themselves or the qualified personnel they would need in order to analyse each case, because there probably are no two identical cases, and this is where the help of the state is needed; I suppose this would be a joint effort by the provinces and the federal government.

Here is the fourth recommendation of this report, and I quote:
Reconciliation procedures are often of great help in restoring marriages that are far from being examples of harmony and stability. Attempts to reconcile the parties should be made part of any legal procedure that deals with marriages that have broken down or are on the verge of a breakdown.
As a layman, Mr. Speaker, I feel that we should have courts specialized in family or marriage matters.
There are family courts in Quebec, but I would rather call them embryos of family courts which are not always headed by competent people, who themselves do not always have counsellors conversant with social, psychological or pedagogical matters. There would be room for much improvement.
But I feel that if the conservation of our natural resources and research in the physical and scientific fields are taken care of, we should first of all, under a priority which, in my opinion, is obvious, invest the amounts needed so that research and organization are made to meet the needs of our human capital.
Married life, family life, marriage are certainly the basis of social life in our country.
I quote again from the same report:
(5) Even if we are not all in complete agreement, it should be noted that, in divorce proceedings, the "matrimonial offences" concept should be replaced by the "breakdown of marriage" concept. This last concept, as explained to the joint committee, answers more adequately the needs of the programs and services which are concerned with the consolidation or rehabilitation of marriages.
Further on, mention is made of federal-provincial co-operation, of which I spoke earlier. This is the conclusion arrived at:
1.	Federal divorce legislation should not play a purely negative role, in the sense that it would merely facilitate the dissolution of already broken marriages.
I spoke about this a little earlier.
2.	The federal government, and all the members of parliament, should be dynamic leaders in promoting and helping the provincial and municipal authorities, as well as the private organizations to have their own legislation, special educational and welfare programs which would supplement the federal policy in order to insure the success of marriages.
It will not be enough, as law-makers, to wash our hands once the divorce legislation is improved. To make it easier in the valid cases, our responsibility must go further than that, that is we must try to prevent the ailment before it becomes acute.

Divorce Law Reform
A third recommendation reads as follows:
3.	If Canada wants adequate marriage programs, its legislation and bills should be submitted to constant inquiries, review and scientific assessment.
At least as much as in material fields.
And I say in closing:
It is the duty of the state to strenghthen marriage and family life.
Mr. Speaker, when considering that bill, certain things strike me. I told you that quite frankly when I admitted that I do not have the legal qualifications of many of my colleagues.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
For instance, under the heading "Grounds", clause 3, page 3 of the bill, it says:
3. Subject to section 5, a petition for divorce may be presented to a court by a husband or wife, on the ground that the respondent, since the celebration of the marriage, (a) has committed adultery:
I find it a little hard to understand that because the husband or wife commits adultery once, the spouse would be justified to ask for an annulment or a divorce. That is beyond me. I am under the impression that if Christ came back on earth, he would show the same generosity he had for the adulteress; he would probably forgive a third and a fourth time and would not be pleased to see a marriage dissolved when there are innocent children, unless the judge should decide, of course, that the situation is becoming extremely serious, which is not the case as a rule, except if the spouse who feels badly treated listens to his or her pride or hurt feelings. I wonder whether we are not opening the door a little too wide. In the past, we complained because adultery could be the only reason for divorce, and we noticed that in a great many cases, the adultery was forged, brought up under false representations. That case still remains.
I find it a little hard to accept that clause, Mr. Speaker. The second paragraph in the same clause states that:
If the respondent has been guilty of sodomy, bestiality or rape, or has engaged in an homosexual act;
Rape, bestiality, sodomy-I have no objection to that because it is against nature. But if we are now prepared to legislate in order to make homosexuality legal, unless it is habitual homosexuality, which has lasted for years and which prevented one of the spouses from fulfilling his or her matrimonial duties, I still think that a distinction should

be made. I imagine, I suppose and I assume that the judge dealing with that case will have enough leeway to say: It has happened once, therefore, it is not grounds for divorce. I do not have the legal competence to pass a final judgment on that but I still submit that it is a matter which impresses me.
There are other grounds a little further, such as for example:
(a) the respondent
(i) has been imprisoned, pursuant to his conviction for one or more offences, for a period or an aggregate period of not less than three years during the five year period immediately preceding the presentation of the petition-
Here again, I suppose that judges would have some discretion, because I could mention cases where a fellow was sentenced to three or four years in prison, but he was not necessarily a bad husband, for all that. But if during that period, the wife gets bored, acquires bad habits which are not in accordance with the requirements of marriage, and if she decides that it would be absolutely necessary to ask for a divorce or a separation, well that would raise problems for the children.
I hope that the judges called upon to settle those cases will not feel bound by the wording of the act which provides three years of imprisonment for adultery and homosexual offences. It is automatic, absolutely cut and dried. They should have enough discretion to say: Since your particular case is not as serious as some others, I shall not allow divorce.
Mr. Speaker, I shall support this bill even though it may be amended, as many of my colleagues have suggested. I suppose that in future years, other amendments will be made to improve it still more, since, for once, this is legislation dealing with such important human problems that year round research and studies should be made in that field and consultation should take place between all competent social and religious organizations, in an attempt to find new formulas.
I repeat it again-it must be repeated, and I am pleased that my colleagues stated it- what has been said in this house in favour of this divorce bill must not be interpreted in the misinformed areas of our country, and that is why it is well that we should say it often, as an approval of divorce as such.
I believe most members, if not all, in this house consider divorce, first for natural reasons, and second, for religious reasons, as inadmissible in principle.
December 15, 1967

In principle, it is evil but we must make allowance for human weakness and consider the fact that we have no right to impose our religious beliefs on those who do not share them. We must also do our utmost to put an end to the old system which fostered hypocrisy, false representations, perjury and a whole lot of things which were denounced in this house.
And we are in good company, since we find that we have the support of religious authorities of almost all religious denominations in Canada. There might be differences of opinion on some details, on such or such a word or condition, but I believe that, on the whole, we have the support of all responsible people who are concerned with the vital cell of society, the family, which will enable the state to survive and to thrive.
It is in this spirit, Mr. Speaker, that I intend to vote in favour of the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am in complete agreement with the purpose of the bill before us, namely, to improve the divorce law of Canada. However, reaction to a number of the provisions of the bill is not good. I believe that the government has in several areas missed an excellent opportunity to make the new divorce law more acceptable to Canadians generally. I believe there was an opportunity to legislate a better definition of the marriage breakdown principle, a better arrangement to bring about reconciliation, and with regard to several other matters with which I shall deal in the course of my remarks.
I say that the government has missed an opportunity because for the first time in many years, following the hearings of the special joint committee which ran over a period of a year, public opinion at this moment is favourable to extending the grounds of divorce to a much greater degree than is the case now. At the same time, the major religious groups in Canada are ready for this type of legislation. Many members of the house who have had reservations in the past are now ready to consider some really profound changes in the divorce law of Canada. Here was an opportunity for the government not only to follow public opinion but perhaps to lead it. I say that in several fields they have missed this opportunity.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Before the bill is passed this situation might be remedied by amending the bill in
Divorce Law Reform
the committee stage at which time the house and the minister will have the opportunity to consider some of the amendments which I believe will be necessary anyway in the next few years and might better be brought in now so that the total jurisprudence on new divorce legislation may be developed at the same time. However, be that as it may, I would say there are several grounds on which the government has completely missed its opportunity.
The first one is on the principle of marriage breakdown. The bill goes so far in accepting marriage breakdown that the government could really leave out matrimonial offences as a ground and extend the definition of marriage breakdown, thus making a uniform divorce law in Canada. Instead, one part of the bill is based on matrimonial offences in which the cause does matter and another part of the bill is based on marriage breakdown in which the cause does not matter. How these two absolutely opposite principles can be blended and a reasonable jurisprudence developed so that the intent of the bill is made clear to the courts and to the people is beyond me. This is why I feel that the opportunity of taking one more step has been missed.
I will not spend much time on the marriage breakdown theory because others have gone into it fairly completely. But I would like to say one word in reply to the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency who spoke a few minutes ago. He said it was his fear that the adoption of marriage breakdown as the sole ground for divorce would make divorce easier. This is a misconception which it took the committee almost a year to clear up, because in many cases divorce would be more difficult to prove in courts.
The fact is that under a satisfactory marriage breakdown system, as recommended by the special joint committee in its draft bill, several safeguards would have to be included. The first one is that reconciliation efforts have been made and can be proven in court in every case. This is not the case under the proposed law and, as I will show later, a simple question put to the applicant in court will settle all the efforts at reconciliation. What we really want is proof that there is no hope of reconciliation and that it has been tried. This is not found in the bill before us.
