grounds of adultery it can be obtained on the proof of a single act of adultery. A divorce which is obtained on only one ground, namely, a matrimonial offence, is what we now call an easy divorce. But it will not be so easy if, in addition to adultery, you have to prove that efforts have been made at reconciliation and that the marriage is at an end and is not likely ever to recover. Finally, in a marriage breakdown bill you would have to provide for care of the children and other ancillary matters to make sure that no one suffers as a result of the divorce.
So I say that marriage breakdown as a ground for divorce would not make divorce easier in a good many cases but would make it more difficult. It would establish to the satisfaction of those interested in the good of society that there is no hope of reconciliation, that all possible efforts have been made, that the marriage is at an end, that the children are provided for, and that the parties are actually and have been living separately for a number of years. In such a case it could never be said that marriage breakdown would make divorce easier. I merely raised that point because it is a misconception which has existed and which was repeated today.
First, I should like to comment on reconciliation procedures. We have heard from the minister and from other members that this bill will provide for procedures for reconciliation of the parties, if there is any hope of this. I say that the bill lacks anything along these lines, and I wish to refer particularly to clause 8. I know that normally we do not refer to specific clauses at this stage of the debate but I wish to quote the wording of the clause because it is important. Clause 8 reads in part as follows:
On a petition for divorce it shall be the duty of the court, before proceeding to the hearing of the evidence, to direct such inquiries to the petitioner and, where the respondent is present, to the respondent as the court deems necessary in order to ascertain whether a possibility exists of their reconciliation-
It goes on to say that if the court believes there is some hope of reconciliation, many possibilities are open for action. The court can adjourn the proceedings, nominate a person to engage in marriage counselling or guidance, and so forth. However, that is only done when the judge feels on examining the parties that there is some hope of reconciliation. Under this bill-and I am sure this will be the case-all that the judge will have to do is to ask the petitioner whether there is

any hope of a reconciliation with the spouse and the only answer necessary in that case will be "no". If such is the answer the judge will have satisfied the statute, and that is all there is to it; all effort will have gone out the window.
Under our present divorce proceedings a number of questions are asked. For example, on condonation the question is asked: Have you forgiven your husband or wife? The petitioner is always warned by counsel of the meaning of this question because a good Christian might think the best answer would be to say that he had forgiven his spouse; she might have erred but he has forgiven her. We know that there will be no divorce if adultery has been condoned. So I am sure that most petitioners seek divorce in the courts with the complete knowledge that they must answer this question correctly. It is a simple question and you can be sure of the answer. When the judge asks you if there is any hope of reconciliation you have to say no. If you say anything else your divorce is delayed or is gone altogether. You must make sure there is no mistake about this.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Clause 7 of the bill provides that counsel must certify he has advised his clients fully upon the opportunities for reconciliation. Counsel cannot even pass by this provision. He cannot even say, I will let this client satisfy the judge on whether or not reconciliation is possible. He will have to advise his client not to say that there is a possibility of reconciliation because the client will not get the divorce. If the client says there is no possibility, the divorce will be granted. I do not believe either the petitioner or counsel will go ahead with a case with the firm intention of having that case thrown out. I cannot see it. If you are going to have any real hope from reconciliation procedures you have to have more than is provided in this bill. There will need to be some other provision than just the necessity for the judge to ask the question, which is all that has to be done at this moment.
This brings me to the next point I want to discuss and it is closely tied to this question of reconciliation. Under these circumstances, we are going to try divorce actions in the high court. They are still going to be on the list for trial at the assizes and there will be half a dozen other cases, civil or criminal. If every trial court does the same thing as is done in Ontario, it will mean the court will try to find half an hour when nothing else is
December 15, 1967

taking place to slip in these divorce actions. Sometimes this occurs when the jury is out considering a criminal case. Sometimes this will occur when there is an adjournment to allow counsel to attempt an agreement in a case. Since there is just a limited amount of time, many of us feel that these cases will be hastened.
We feel, therefore, that county and district courts should be permitted to handle divorces. County and district court judges, except in the larger centres, are always available. They will be there today, tomorrow and next week and so will have some time to give thought to the question of reconciliation. They will not just pass off the question of reconciliation with a simple question as the high court judges are going to do. I know, just as sure as I am standing here, this is what the high court judges will do. They will put the simple question: Is there any hope of reconciliation? The answer will be no. If the judge has nothing else to do he may take some time to probe, but in the normal case the judge will just ask the question. The high court judge will be anxious to get these cases off his list. If he receives the right answer to that simple question the case will be disposed of. The high court judge will not want to be tied up with the question of reconciliation because he will move to another assize next week and may not be back to that centre for two years. Counsel would have to chase him around to another centre or try to find another judge, and in some cases may have to wait until the next time the judge is in that place.
Under those circumstances what hope is there for reconciliation? I believe for all these reasons that this bill is absolutely useless, especially in so far as the reconciliation procedure is concerned. The fact that county courts are not being given jurisdiction in these cases means there is no hope of people pursuing the possibility of reconciliation if that would be helpful. I say, therefore, that the bill falls short of what many of us thought it would do.
I should like to follow up the other question about county courts because their use is not related just to the reconciliation procedures. The special joint committee gave this matter a lot of thought. We heard a lot of witnesses. When the minister made his introductory remarks I asked him why the county and district courts had not been given jurisdiction under this bill. He gave two answers. He said, first, that we were dealing with the fundamental rights of people which should
27053-347J

be settled in the high court and, second, that jurisprudence would be built up over the years and this should be done in a high court. I should like to deal with these two matters.
In the first place, I have already mentioned the question of reconciliation and of marriage breakdown. There is in addition the question of cost, and this is an even greater reason for putting these divorces into county courts. Under this bill we are trying to make divorces available to those whose marriages have broken down and for whom there is no hope of reconciliation. Many of these people cannot now obtain a divorce and in some cases they cannot afford it. If we could put these divorce actions into county and district courts, the tariffs and fees in those courts are half of what they are in the supreme court. While we are trying to make divorces more available to Canadians under this bill, regardless of their ability to pay, at the same time we are keeping divorce actions in the superior courts to which these people cannot afford to go. It has been pointed out on several occasions that if there is any possibility of reconciliation the procedures established under this bill that counsel will have to undertake will be monumental. These procedures are going to shove up the cost. The procedures are not those that can be undertaken by social workers or by other people engaged in this type of activity at public expense. These procedures, in a large measure, are going to have to be carried out by a lawyer. When a lawyer starts a case, therefore, he will start it with the possibility of reconciliation procedures in mind.
This same situation exists now in the province of Ontario with regard to children. If there are children involved in divorce proceedings you have to go through an ancillary procedure under which you need a report from the official guardian with regard to the maintenance of the children. We know, therefore, that a divorce involving children is going to take more time and is therefore going to be more expensive.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Under the new bill there are three possibilities. First, there is the possibility that during the trial or before judgment absolute the court will find that reconciliation procedures would be helpful. In that case, Mr. Speaker, the judge would order a review of the whole case and the court would have to be satisfied that there was no possibility of reconciliation.

December 15, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
So, Mr. Speaker, bearing in mind that not only is there the question of divorce but also the welfare of the children and reconciliation possibilities to be considered, the cost of a divorce action would be difficult to determine because there could be an extended hearing which might last months or even years. This is particularly so should the action reach the supreme court where higher fees are quoted. In this connection some assistance has been given in Ontario through the introduction of legal aid; however, legal aid is not universal throughout the country.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, for these reasons I think the bill has not met the objective parliament hoped to achieve. It has not followed in its terms the major recommendation made by the committee in cases where there is a possibility of the marriage being revived.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment on the two answers given by the minister regarding county court jurisdiction. This goes beyond the question of cost and reconciliation proceedings, but the minister did deal with the two other fundamental points. First of all he said that in divorce cases the courts would be dealing with the fundamental rights of individuals and therefore felt that this was a matter for the superior courts.
Judges of the county and district courts are drawn from the legal profession of the provinces. County and district courts deal at times with very substantial matters. They settle very real legal questions and, with one or two exceptions, actually have concurrent jurisdiction with the high court. Nevertheless I have never heard it said that the county and district courts did not deal with fundamental rights. Certainly they hear jury cases, and the judges try criminal offences either with or without a jury. So surely fundamental rights are involved in the county and district courts, the judges of which can deal with almost any crime except murder, and some other serious offences. Therefore I do not think the minister has put forward a valid reason for not trying divorce cases in these courts.
The second reason offered by the minister was that jurisprudence should be settled in the high courts. Although I would agree with this statement, I think it is well known that jurisprudence is mostly settled in the appellate courts, not in the trial division. In cases involving interpretation of statutes it is almost certain that one of the parties will appeal the decision, and it is the appeal court that settles the question.

I therefore see no difference between an appellate court hearing an appeal from a county court and hearing an appeal from a high court. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the appeal procedure in county court cases is almost identical to that in high court cases. While I think a case may be made for saying that jurisprudence is settled in the higher courts, I do not see this as a valid objection in this instance. Against that there are the other disadvantages of the county court system to which I have already referred.
One final word about county courts, Mr. Speaker. They are in most cases much more closely in contact with the social agencies in the area. If the court decides that in a given case reconciliation procedures will be of assistance, while the county or district judge would know the appropriate agency to which to refer the parties, I am sure a high court judge on circuit would not have the same information. He would therefore have to turn to someone, perhaps the sheriff of the county or to counsel themselves, and would have to decide which was the most suitable body in the area to deal with the case. For example, in one district or county it might be the Children's Aid Society. In another area it might be a welfare agency. In yet another it might be a clergyman or some other person who has had reasonable success with rehabilitation and reconciliation procedures. Therefore, I contend that the county or district courts are better equipped than the supreme court in this particular exercise.
I think I should give the minister warning now-though he probably has received it- that we intend to move some amendments after the bill has been given second reading. Certainly I hope he will give serious thought to the question I have raised, otherwise the value of the bill will not only be diminished but divorce will be made more expensive, thus detracting from the very purpose of the bill in the modern context of today, which is to make divorce more accessible to those in dire need.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks on Bill C-187. It has been said that this bill is the best centennial and Christmas gift to the 500,000 Canadians who are living under common law marriages that the government has produced this year. The introduction of this legislation has also produced the feeling among Canadians that the government is
December 15, 1967

determined to restore the institution of marriage and to give it its necessary moral, physical and spiritual well-being.
It would be very easy for me to give the full credit and glory to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) for bringing forth this measure at this time, but I think we would be doing an injustice if we did not recall the efforts of previous pioneers in the matter of divorce reform. When one thinks of the active work undertaken by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) in forcing the government to stop rubber stamping divorces, and to send them to the exchequer court, making the Senate finally responsible for the decrees, he realizes the courage and foresight that these two particular members possessed.
One would like also to recall the suggestion the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) made some time ago to the effect that divorce cases be dealt with by the exchequer court. It would also be unfair not to give a great deal of credit to the communications media, to churches and other organized public opinion bodies throughout Canada who have brought this social issue to the forefront and forced the government to take action.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons performed yeoman service in studying this problem and it would be fair to say its report forms the basis of the bill we have before us. I was not a member of that committee, but from my reading of the report it appears to me that the main issue was between those who advocate an approach by way of matrimonial offences as grounds for divorce and those who believe in the marriage breakdown theory. The former set up a list of matrimonial offences and rely on the judicial adversary system for proof thereof before a divorce is granted. Proponents of the marriage breakdown theory rely on the inquisitorial approach; the separation of the parties forms the basis for the action and the court proceeds to determine whether there has been an irretrievable marriage breakdown. If this is found to be the case, then if adequate provision has been made for the wife, the children, and in some instances for the husband, a divorce is granted.
Under the marriage breakdown theory great emphasis is placed on reconciliation. The government in its wisdom has combined both approaches, the major emphasis being
Divorce Law Reform
placed on the matrimonial offence approach. The government shied away from the marriage breakdown principle because it was felt the courts would be given an indefinite and uncontrolled discretion, and preferred marriage breakdown to be established by proof of specific matrimonial offences.
Although I agree with the matrimonial breakdown principle, I must say the attitude which has been taken by the government appears to me to be proper at this time. I believe that in Canada we are not yet ready to accept in its complete form the marriage breakdown theory. Hon. members who have supported it have pointed to the examples of England and Australia. I would remind them that England is reaching its present attitude in two stages. Back in 1937 the government amended the divorce laws so as to include many of the matrimonial offences which are set out in the bill before us. Now Britain is ready to take a second step by recognizing the principle of matrimonial breakdown.
I would remind the house, too, that the English courts are specialized. Divorce petitions are heard in the divorce and admiralty court; criminal cases are heard separately; civil cases are heard separately. These courts are presided over by judges who specialize in particular fields of law, and judicial appointments to the bench are made bearing in mind the particular aspects of the law to be considered. We in Canada, on the other hand, appoint as our judges lawyers who have had experience both as solicitors and as counsel, and it seems to me we might not have available the specialized experience on the bench which would be required if the marriage breakdown theory were adopted.
Then again, I believe application of the marriage breakdown principle would leave too much room for interpretation and discretion on the part of the judges. Decisions could vary widely, and become highly unpredictable. Precedents would have to be built up in connection with many of the matrimonial offences to be considered. In other words, we might find that as the matrimonial offences theory is cast out of the front door by the legislature, it creeps into the back door of the courthouse.
Another reason advanced in support of the marriage breakdown principle has been the sordidness attached to proving adultery. I suggest it may be even more embarrassing or humiliating to proceed on the basis of marriage breakdown than it is at present, or than it would be under the terms of Bill C-187.

December 15, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
I can only speak from my own experience in the practice of law in Ontario. What I have found is that 98 per cent of all divorce cases are undefended and that no more than 5 per cent or 10 per cent are concerned with detective evidence. In the great majority of cases the action is approached on a so-called friendly basis; there is an absence of the humiliation and embarrassment to which some hon. members have referred.
Some have said there is a great deal of fabrication attached to evidence given in divorce actions. My experience has been that the judges of the supreme court are mature in their approach and can detect quite easily any fabricated evidence. In most instances it is not necessary to present evidence of catching a defendant in the act of adultery. Usually the evidence which is presented is evidence of past adultery which has been reported by one of the parties to the solicitor of the other party.
All one needs to do with regard to proving adultery in Ontario is to lay the foundation upon which an inference can be drawn that adultery has been committed. So there is a minimum of bitterness and humiliation. Ontario courts also require a report from the official guardian setting forth particulars with regard to the parties and the circumstances in which they are living, in order to give full protection to the wife and provide for the maintenance and custody of the children.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
My criticism of the marriage breakdown basis is that an undue weight would inevitably be placed on the independent evidence of social workers and experts in marriage counselling. It is not clear whether the court would be called upon to take the mandatory or discretionary approach with regard to the procedure of reconciliation, and so social workers would be placed in the very awkward position of having to take sides with regard to the presentation of the evidence, and their function as social workers would be greatly impaired.
Again with respect to the marriage breakdown theory, the basis of the separation approach, it is said that once the separation has been established the court must determine whether the marriage is irretrievably broken down. In fact, in the committee report, as recorded at page 121, four questions are set forth as follows:
Firstly, has the marriage broken down? Secondly, if so, are there any reasonable prospects of

reconciliation? Thirdly, if not, is there any reason of public policy, especially involving the parties of the children, why the divorce should be denied? And finally, if not, what arrangements should be made regarding the parties and the children?
By the suggested procedure, on proof of a period of separation alone, the court would be prepared to assume a positive answer to the question: has the marriage broken down; and in the absence of evidence to the country, it would assume similarly that reconciliation is not reasonably likely and that there is no reason to withhold the divorce. If there was anything in the evidence that led the court to believe reconciliation was possible, it could adjourn the case for an attempt to be made, but unless the fact of the marriage breakdown was strongly disputed by one of the parties, there would be no inquest to establish that the marriage had irretrievably broken down. . . Probably the only occasion for a full inquest into a marriage would be when a wife opposed it on the grounds that it would bring hardship upon her and her children, despite the fact that a husband had made quite an equitable arrangement. These cases would probably be few and the courts would be able to cope with them without any undue strain.
In this type of case you find one of the parties disputing the breakdown of the marriage. Advocates of the separation theory have said the separation term should be three years, but that may not be a sufficient period to bring about any reconciliation of the parties with regard to matrimonial offences. If a matrimonial offence has been an outrageous one, then possibly the period of three years may be too long. Some of the recommendations that were made covered periods ranging from two years to seven years. It is very difficult to determine an exact period with regard to the separation, and that may be the reason why it would be unwise to have separation as a sole and comprehensive ground.

I think my colleague appreciates the position I am placed in, that basically I believe in the marriage breakdown theory, but I find many practical difficulties presented by it. It may be, as he says, that if there has been an outrageous matrimonial offence within the three year period, then that period would be more than sufficient.

Now, directing my mind to the bill, Mr. Speaker, there are certain provisions which I am very happy to see in it. One is the extension of the matrimonial offences, and the combination of the two approaches covering matrimonial offences and the breakdown theory. The second is the provision which would have the effect of abolishing parliamentary divorce by setting up temporarily a new divorce division of the Exchequer Court of Canada, and enabling the jurisdiction to be transferred to the superior court of Quebec and the supreme court of Newfoundland.
The third provision in the bill which makes me happy is that respecting domicile. Practising lawyers appreciate the problems they have faced in the past with regard to domicile, especially where the husband had deserted. An attempt was made in 1930, through the Divorce Jurisdiction Act, to give the wife a limited break, but the provision in this bill goes far beyond that and it is certainly a most welcome one.
Next comes the question of the disappearance of one of the spouses to a marriage. In Ontario we had the situation that if one of the spouses could not find the other, after a period of six or seven years that party could apply under the Ontario marriage act for a marriage licence, and if, after reasonable inquiries were made, proof was offered that the other spouse could not be found, a licence was granted to marry a second time.
However, such people were always under the cloud that the first husband or wife might turn up, and this is not a very happy basis for a marriage. Further, the children of the second marriage were placed in a very awkward position if the first husband returned and the second marriage was declared to be void.
Of course there are shortcomings with regard to the bill. The first has been elaborated on by most hon. members, and it concerns the jurisdiction of the county courts. One would think the government would be happy to accept the county court jurisdiction as concurrent with that of the supreme court. Able argument has been presented by hon. members to show that small towns may be visited by judges on circuit only three or four times a year, and also the difficulty this causes in modifying maintenance agreements.
The question of costs is very important, and one would think that the costs in a county court would be much less than they
Divorce Law Reform
are in a supreme court. One cannot help but be impressed with the evidence given to the joint committee by the former chief justice of Ontario. He gave that committee the benefit of his experience and recommended that there should be concurrent jurisdiction.
I would like to draw the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) to clause 3(d) where there is set forth certain conduct as a basis for a petition for divorce. This includes "sodomy, bestiality or rape, or has engaged in a homosexual act." One would think that lesbian acts should also be included. I think that is a shortcoming with respect to this particular provision in the bill. Another shortcoming concerns the question of adultery, where there is artificial insemination without the consent of the husband. These are provisions which probably will have to be amended in the future, and it may be necessary to incorporate new clauses now.
I also draw the minister's attention to clause 4(a)(i) dealing with imprisonment as the basis of a petition for divorce. It reads at present that the respondent-
-has been imprisoned, pursuant to his conviction for one or more offences, for a period or an aggregate period of not less than three years during the five year period immediately preceding the presentation of the petition,-

One finds that in criminal law there are many sentences for two years less a day. So in respect of that sentence which sends a person to a reformatory in the particular province, one would have to determine whether two years less a day would constitute really two years time. A person could be convicted to two years less a day on one offence and be convicted for one year determinate on a second offence. In this case the petitioner would have the difficulty of not complying with the three year period because of the provision of two years less a day. I should like to direct the minister's attention to that particular sentence because it may be that some clarification is necessary with regard to this type of problem.
I should like to draw the minister's attention to another clause with regard to desertion, which says:
...by reason of the desertion of the petitioner for a period of not less than five years...
I note that under the Australian law the period in respect of desertion is two years. It

Divorce Law Reform
would seem to me that the five year period might create quite a hardship. In Australia, where they have adopted the marriage breakdown theory and where they have set forth 16 types of situations, we find that the period is two years. One thing which I am sure is in the minds of many members and many other Canadians is the problem of the possible flood of divorce actions in the next three years in the Ontario courts. Therefore I thought it might be wise to read about the experience in Australia, where they have standardized their divorce procedure. I should like to refer to an article in the Toronto Daily Star of April 29, 1967 by Geoffrey Tebbutt, which in part reads as follows:
The standardization of the law and its liberalization in some important ways has not resulted in any startling increase in divorce.
The number of dissolutions, nullities and judicial separations in Australia in the decade before the uniform divorce laws averaged 6,973 a year. There was a small drop to 6,750 in 1961, the first year of the uniform divorce law.
Since then, the figures have been 1962, 7.290: 1963, 7,513; 1964, 7.967; and 1965 , 8,534. The upward trend is largely due to population growth.
The single ground most frequently cited in Australian divorces in 1965 was desertion (3,777 cases), followed by adultery (2,035 cases) and separation (1,706 cases).
Mr. Speaker, this should give some encouragement and some consolation to people who think we will be flooded with divorce actions. When one realizes that there are 500,000 common law marriages in Canada at the moment he also must realize that if people are to put their matrimonial house in order there probably will be an increase for a certain period to take care of the problem and to restrengthen the institution of marriage.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to give the Minister of Justice credit for his courage and his initiative in bringing forth this bill at this particular time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might say at the very beginning that despite the shortcomings of this very important piece of social legislation I intend to support it. In all probability I shall vote for it on second reading. I take this position despite the fact that I am one who believes that a valid marriage cannot be dissolved by any civil authority. However, I must say I do not expect to impose my beliefs on all the people of Canada. The power of the civil authorities to dissolve a marriage is now an

established fact in our society. I do not expect that the laws of this country should be framed in such a way that they would prevent from obtaining a divorce those who in good faith do not believe that marriage is indissoluble.
I was privileged to be a member of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons which heard the representations made by various organizations which appeared before it. There certainly seemed to be broad general agreement on the need for legislative reforms which will provide more adequate social means to deal with marital problems. Those of us who listened to the testimony could not help but be impressed by the fact that unfortunately there are today some marriages which in fact are a hell on earth. We were very often reminded of the heartbreak and sometimes physical cruelty which results from such marriages. For those who find themselves in this unfortunate situation and believe in divorce, there should be some relief.
However, in our enthusiasm to provide this relief by a reform of our divorce laws we must not lose sight of the fact that lifelong marriage is the ideal, and that suits for divorce must be the last resort in the case of apparently broken marriages. We must not forget that the family is still the basic unit of society and that any forces which tend to destroy that basic unit are the enemies of men, and must be recognized as such. I believe we will all admit that a stable marriage is preferable to divorce.
It had been my hope that the proposed legislation would have made some provision to help promote stable marriages. In our desire to give relief in deserving cases we must not abandon our efforts on behalf of happy homes. I suggest that this is of direct concern to parliament. I suggest further that any further changes in the divorce law should be related to measures which have as their objective the fostering of stable marriages.
It is true that the present legislation does provide measures for reconciliation procedures but, as already suggested here today, I am afraid these will not be very effective. Clause 7 of the bill provides that the solicitor who is acting for the parties is required to draw to the attention of his client the provisions of the act which have as their object the bringing about of a reconciliation. He is
December 15, 1967



obliged under this clause to inform his client that marriage counselling assistance might be available to him. He is obliged to discuss with his client the possibility of reconciliation. I suggest, however, that this may very easily become merely a matter of routine. The solicitor will do it simply because he is required to do it. That in itself does not guarantee a reconciliation.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I followed very carefully the proceedings of the committee and tried to analyze the more than 1700 pages of evidence, which I think represents every shade of opinion. It would appear to me that six major points evolved from these hearings and I should like to place these on record. The first is the need for reform of our present law. I do not think there is any question about the fact that everyone who appeared before the committee agreed that the present laws need reform. The measure now before us is a step in the right direction, and while I do not entirely agree with it I am prepared to support it because it is a reform of what we now have on the statute books.
The second point is that suits for divorce should be the last resort. This was also recognized by practically everyone who testified at the committee hearings. The third point is that at times even the best of marriages, as they pass through various stages, require counselling services. These services should be available to all Canadians.
I realize that to provide such services will present problems, inasmuch as people who are properly qualified to give these services may not be readily available. Something should be done to encourage more people to take up this profession so that counselling services can be made available when required. The fourth point is that reconciliation procedures are often necessary and often effective in rebuilding marriages that are on the brink of destruction. Reconciliation attempts should therefore be a part of any legal proceedings dealing with faltering or broken marriages. The fifth point is that there is impressive, if not complete agreement that the marriage breakdown concept should replace that of marital offences in divorce proceedings. This has been adequately dealt with by other speakers. I personally would prefer to see the marriage breakdown concept supplanted as the only ground for divorce, rather than retaining the various things set out in the measure.
Divorce Law Reform
I do not think it is true that the marriage breakdown concept will lead to more divorces or make divorce easier, and I think this concept was recognized by most of those who appeared before the committee as the one more likely to relate properly to the necessity for divorce, rather than the specific things mentioned in the present law, or this bill.
The sixth and final point was in relation to the need for specialized courts to handle divorce cases. That point was clearly brought out by a number of people and organizations who presented briefs and gave evidence. I am fully cognizant of the many difficulties involved in this matter. There are constitutional questions which have to be taken into consideration. Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at any length at this stage of the bill, nor is it my intention to enter into a discussion of the details contained therein. However, I do want to make a few brief comments in a general sense regarding the matter that is now before the house. I followed with a great deal of interest the minister's statement when introducing this measure, which proposes to make some fundamental changes in Canada's divorce laws.
We all know that for some time this subject has exercised the minds of a great many Canadians. Many have vociferously urged divorce reform while others have viewed such reform with some misgivings. Those who tend to oppose reform in our divorce legislation do so, not because they desire to inflict further unhappiness on those concerned but because they view the trend as a threat to the established and divinely ordained institution of the family and the home, which in turn is recognized as the very foundation of our society and our nation.
Therefore the introduction of this legislation will meet with a mixed reception across the country, even though many members have stated that the country in general is more than ready to accept fundamental changes in our divorce laws. Personally I cannot share the undisguised joy with which some members of this house have greeted the measure. I have been rather surprised at the almost unanimous support that has been indicated. As I have pointed out, some have referred to this legislation in very glowing terms, even to the extent that it will be a wonderful Christmas present for a great many people. It seems to me that we have now reached the point where we have some very queer ideas about Christmas and Christmas presents. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do not think this legislation would fit into the category that has been attached to it.

I have a copy of the brief, as have all hon. members no doubt, that was presented to the House of Commons committee on divorce by the Congress of Canadian Women on June 27, 1966. I should like to read just two sentences which are to be found on the first page of the brief:
Divorce is a social devil, a disease symptom of a society that is ill. The remedy does not lie in making divorce more difficult but in seeking out the causes and as much as possible in removing them.
I am not indicating that this brief is opposed to the suggestions of divorce reform, but I wanted to place on record this particular definition of divorce because I believe it is something that should cause us some uneasiness as we deal with the legislation that is before us.
I do not believe that divorce reform will be the cure-all for the social problems that face us. Mention has been made of a number of these problems, such as illegitimacy, so many people living in a common law relationship, and many other things. Hon. members have spoken about the unhappiness that is inherent in a situation where love has departed and the relationship has settled down to more or less an endurance proposition.
I do not believe that divorce will solve all these problems. I am not so naive as to believe that if we make it easier for people to obtain a divorce there will not be common law relationships, because we find that a great many of these relationships are formed even if there is no impediment to marriage. Therefore, making divorce easier to obtain will not meet this particular problem. It will not mean that those who obtain a divorce and then remarry will be happy.
I think we all know of a great many cases where people have been divorced and have remarried three, four, five or six times and still have not been happy. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this measure will not be a cure-all as far as the unhappiness of certain individuals is concerned. I acknowledge, however, that there are those who will benefit by changes and amendments to our divorce laws. But this measure certainly will not meet the situation in every case.
I believe it should be a source of great concern to us that we have failed in our endeavour to promote and maintain a society that is built on the concept of the sacredness and permanence of the marriage relationship.
Divorce Law Reform
I think if we viewed the question from this point of view it would take some of the jubilation out of us as far as the introduction of this measure is concerned.
My attitude to the bill before the house does not involve a choice between what I conceive to be right and what I conceive to be wrong. I am forced into the position where I have to make a decision between what I consider to be two evils, on the one hand divorce and on the other the regrettable tragedy of legal relationships without meaning. Therefore in making my decision with regard to this matter I have to choose the lesser of the two evils.
Having voiced these fears, and while my understanding of the moral and spiritual laws as outlined in the Bible require that those of us who accept its authority govern ourselves accordingly, I am constrained to acknowledge the validity of the argument advanced by many in this house and by the minister in his introduction of the bill, namely that we must recognize the difficulty of applying what may be ecclesiastical, religious law to what the minister has termed a secular, or I believe he used the word profane, society.
As I have pointed out, it is not my intention to deal at this time with the various provisions of the bill. I wanted to indicate to the house that we are not unanimous by any means in approval of the measure that is before us; at least we are not in full agreement as far as its general concept is concerned.

In my view it is wrong under these circumstances to compel people, who have lost the love and respect for each other which brought them together in the first place, to continue that relationship when they no longer have the basis on which the marriage was built in the first place.

I think that divorce is an essential measure which we must keep up to date as we do other measures in other fields. He said: The purpose of this bill is to revive the old common law offence of eavesdropping. I introduced this bill because of my concern and the concern of an increasingly large number of people in this country about what we believe to be a pernicious practice. This practice has been followed by law enforcement agencies, private investigators and probably other interested people who have invaded the privacy of ordinary citizens for personal reasons through the use of more and more highly sophisticated equipment. This practice used to be called wire tapping but the equipment used is now so sophisticated it does not require the physical tapping of the wires.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, is very similar, with small amendments, to the bill introduced in this house several sessions ago by the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) when he sat as a private member. We in Canada have traditionally looked upon ourselves as being very moral people. We have been quick to condemn the very antisocial activities in other countries such as the United States. One of the subjects upon which we have seen frequent reports in Canadian newspapers and magazines has been this question of wire tapping in the United States, the interception of telephone conversations. These articles suggest that is a common thing in the United States. Until recently this practice was reported in Canadian newspapers as if it were something which did not happen in Canada. The facts of course are entirely different. As they have become known in recent years, the facts prove that in every province of Canada there is no doubt taking place what we commonly call wire tapping.
On other occasions when I have introduced this bill I have given some illustrations. I
Criminal Code
will go over them quickly today because I do not believe there is any need to put all of the details on the record. I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, and I repeat, that I am satisfied on the basis of information I have received and which I consider to be accurate, that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police used wire tapping extensively in Montreal at the time they were investigating the bombing carried on by the F.L.Q. I said before, and I say again, that this was a very serious situation, so one cannot blame the police for taking all the steps which were required. The point I made before, and which I make again, is that if the parliament of Canada believes wire tapping is necessary, then the law should be amended to make clear that wire tapping by the police is permissible and legal, and any restrictions or limitations upon it should be spelled out.
If hon. members doubt that the R.C.M.P. carries on the practice of wire tapping, I refer them to an article which appeared in the Toronto Star of August 31, 1966, written by Robert Reguly. I am sure most members will know him as a very aggressive, successful and accurate reporter. I should like to quote a couple of paragraphs from this article:
For the R.C.M.P. has a discreet liaison with the Bell wiretap-checking branch in Montreal. The three Bell men there who check for wiretap are ex-mounties, according to a former Bell official.
Later, in the same article, I read:
S.I. maintains a wiretap installation in one of the major downtown Montreal hotels, enabling it to tap any room phone.
Another Montreal hotel-and one in downtown Toronto-are notorious for susceptibility to mount-ie wiretapping.
It is a very frightening thing, if it is true and I believe it is true, to think that if a member of parliament or any other citizen happens to be at these hotels his telephone conversation may be overheard. I know for a fact, Mr. Speaker, that during the S.I.U. investigation by the R.C.M.P. a hotel room in Toronto was set up so the R.C.M.P. could listen to conversations taking place. It is now an established fact of record that in Saskatoon the one telephone

-he must put an end to this practice, for the force is breaking the law. He should also announce this action to parliament and the country.

Nevertheless, if those who are charged with the administration of justice do believe it is necessary, then I suggest they ought not to carry it on injudiciously, refusing to admit it is being carried on, hoping to get by, and that the public will ignore it. They at least ought to have the honesty to report such cases to the minister; and the minister ought to bring in legislation which would make it clear, as I think my bill does, that wire tapping is prohibited except in certain special circumstances, anti these circumstances should be detailed.
It may be that I would not agree with the reasons given by the minister for permitting wire tapping, but at least the matter could be discussed by parliament. Then if wire tapping were permitted it would only be on the condition that the police went to a judge of the superior court, gave reasons for the wire tapping and obtained a court order. In addition, Mr. Speaker, a report should be made once a year, as I understand is the case in Great Britain, of the number of times the authority given the police by the law had been exercised.

I recognized the validity of my hon. friend's reasons then for not wanting to pass that legislation in the form in which it was submitted. What I did not understand was his failure to have these bills or their subject matter brought before a parliamentary committee. I regret that the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) is not in the house at the moment because I intend to suggest that in the next session, at least, if not in the present one, this kind of study should be made by a parliamentary committee.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North in presenting his most inadequate bill gave the impression that approval had been given to it by the civil liberties committee of the Canadian Bar Association. If he had done his homework he would know that this is not the case. What has happened, as I understand it, is this: Last fall a report was made to the annual general meeting of the Canadian Bar Association in the form of a resolution far broader than that suggested by the hon. member. My information is that it was in these terms:
(1)	All electronic eavesdropping be made a criminal offence with the proviso that electronic eavesdropping may be employed by law enforcement agencies under judicial control.
(2)	Electronic eavesdropping shall not be permitted under any circumstances to interfere with privileged communications.
(3)	Electronic eavesdropping shall only be authorized in circumstances analogous to those under which a peace officer has the right to arrest without warrant.
(4)	Evidence obtained through the illegal use of electronic eavesdropping shall not be made admissible in any court of law.
(5)	Any charge before any court, the investigation of which has in the opinion of the court been furthered by means of wilful disregard of the provisions against electronic eavesdropping shall be dismissed, unless the court is of the opinion that such a dismissal would not be in the interest of justice.
I understand that this resolution was not adopted by the Canadian Bar Association
[Mr. Orlikow.l
because a majority of the members present for the closing session were of the opinion that there was not then sufficient time to consider properly a matter of such importance. However, I believe it will be considered at the next annual meeting and it is intended that a copy of the resolution will be circulated well in advance so that a full discussion might take place. I am informed that a half day of the general meeting will be set aside for the sole purpose of considering this resolution. This gives some indication of the importance attached to it by the Canadian Bar Association.
It is clear that the hon. member for Winnipeg North has scarcely scratched the surface of this problem in his minimal approach to it. If one looks back to the report of those who studied this subject for the benefit of the civil liberties section of the Canadian Bar Association, one finds that as far back as 1965 the chairman of that group, Mr. Aubrey E. Golden, in a report he submitted on September 2 of that year set out what he and his group felt were minimum requirements for legislation. I should like to quote from this report.
It is my respectful submission that only one federal enactment is required. It must be such that it constructs an effective balance between the interest of the individual citizen in maintaining his privacy and the right of the state to secure itself against crime or unlawful activity.
Federal legislation should absolutely prohibit eavesdropping and wire-tapping and make only rigidly defined exceptions where the interest of the state appears to be paramount.

(a)	the offence being investigated must be an indictable offence;
(b)	normal methods of investigation must have been tried and failed, or must, from the nature of things, be unlikely to succeed if tried;
(c)	there must be good reason to think that an interception would result in a conviction;
(d)	where the identity of the person sought to be convicted is known, that no other charge is pending against him.
Mr. Golden in his report goes on to examine in some detail the considerations which should enter into the drafting of such legislation. He states it should be an offence
December 15, 1967

to divulge any confidential communication between counsel and client which may happen to be overheard by anyone. He suggests that any kind of approved eavesdropping and wire tapping activities should be limited to a period before the actual charge is laid. He suggests that the only reasonable sanction for failure to observe any restriction which might be placed in the Criminal Code concerning wire tapping or eavesdropping would be the automatic dismissal of any resulting charge in the event that it follows any unauthorized activity. In addition, he suggests, violation of such legislation should be made an indictable offence, with severe minimum penalties provided.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Mr. Golden in this report stresses the fact that we must sanctify the right of privacy with strong legislative action, and only then should we recognize a carefully defined and safeguarded procedure which will assist our law enforcement agencies. He points out that both the United States and Great Britain have held public inquiries, with some educational effect, on the questions of wire tapping, eavesdropping and the invasion of privacy, but in Canada this has not been done.
I agree with Mr. Golden that it is difficult to see how truly effective legislation can be enacted by a government until it is in possession of such basic facts as would indicate where eavesdropping is most useful to law enforcement agencies, and until it has a definition of the real civil liberties issue. I submit that there should be such an inquiry where all interested parties could make submissions, and the issue be put into perspective for government and public alike.
In the United States there have been hearings on this subject over the past two years. Since last March the subcommittee on administrative practice and procedure, headed by Senator Edward V. Long, Democrat, of Missouri, has held hearings on a right of privacy bill. The first witness to be heard at those hearings was the attorney general of the United States, Ramsey Clark. Those hearings continued until October last when the bill was referred to the senate judiciary committee. At that time the Missouri senator in a press statement said:
This bill is essential if we are going to clear up the legal fog that now surrounds wire tapping, eavesdropping, and snooping in America. I think Congress owes it to the citizens of this nation to act on this measure as soon as possible.
Criminal Code
This right of privacy bill would prohibit all wire tapping or mechanical bugging except with the consent of one party. However, an exception is made for the President of the United States to authorize the use of these devices where the national security is threatened. It would also prohibit the manufacture, shipment, and advertising of all devices in interstate commerce which are designed for wire tapping and electronic snooping.
Another prominent American who has spoken out on the subject is Senator Robert F. Kennedy, Democrat, of New York, who in a speech before the law school forum at Columbia University last year said that all modern technology must be used in fighting crime, and he added:
At the same time, however, we must act to assure that the new technology serves us properly and does not invade the privacy of the individual.
That should surely be the purpose of any legislation on this subject which is passed by this house. We should be much more ambitious in our attempt to attack this most modern of problems than has been the hon. member for Winnipeg North. Our purpose in reform in this field should surely be to protect truly the little man from the big ear.
It is clear from previous debates in the house on this subject that corporations and wealthy persons can protect themselves from electronic snoopers with counter devices which are almost as sophisticated as those available for snooping. There is, in fact, no legal restriction in Canadian law against the manufacture, sale or use of electronic devices for either snooping or the detection of snooping. This is a very grave lack in the law which should preserve the rights of Canadians to privacy.
In stressing the importance of a broad brush approach to such reform I would like to refer again to an editorial which my hon. friend from Winnipeg North mentioned in support of this bill; but when he hears my quotation from it, I think he will recognize it in fact as a clear denunciation of his approach. This editorial in the Toronto Star of September 5, 1964, included the following statement:
What is needed is an amendment to the Criminal Code that would ban all electronic or mechanical eavesdropping. The only exception would be made for police eavesdropping with the permission of a superior court judge.
That obviously goes far beyond what the hon. member is proposing in his bill.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to be here again debating with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). In a time of continuing change in the political situation of Canada, it is always reassuring that there will be occasions like this when he will reintroduce the bill he has introduced for many years past and I in turn will have the opportunity to speak about it.
Several things have occurred in the useful relationship he and I have had in this regard. The first, dealing with eavesdropping, has been the appearance of intruders in this field. I am pleased to have the participation and the assistance of the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury), and I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North must be equally delighted to have the support of that pillar of ultramontane society, the doyen of manners and morals in this house, that defender of king and empire, the eloquent and articulate member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), who has introduced the bill which immediately follows that of the hon. member on the order paper, dealing with this same subject matter.
Therefore we will have the opportunity not only of discussing the type of law which the hon. member for Winnipeg North thinks is appropriate here-and for reasons I will deal with later, which I think is inappropriate-but in the near future and I think I can predict a time of not less than an hour, we will have the opportunity of discussing at great length, the legislative proposal being put forward by the hon. member for Kootenay West.

The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) tells me he thinks I should express a little praise also for the members who have stayed to listen to this debate, and I am quite prepared to recognize their participation in that manner over the years.
e (5:40 p.m.)
I have given an undertaking to the hon. member for Winnipeg North not to refer to any of the material I used in previous years, or for example to the fact that his political friends may have engaged in these self-same practices in Saskatchewan. I take it as accepted that that has occurred, and therefore I will not go further into the question. I should like to introduce into the debate what I believe has been perhaps a useful addition to the public documents on this subject. This has become available since we last discussed this matter. I am referring to the report of the Commission of Inquiry into Invasion of Privacy. The hearings of this commission were conducted by Commissioner R. A. Sargent in the province of British Columbia, and the report is dated August 9, 1967. As I believe hon. members are aware this had to do not so much with telephonic wire tapping as with bugging or eavesdropping which had been engaged in during the course of a union dispute.
The first conclusion to which the commissioner came, as the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) has already said, was that there was no question that the union official, Mr. O'Neal, was involved in any illegal conduct. In fact there is no criminal law and I do not believe there is any civil law in Canada-although I should not speak for a jurisdiction where I am not a member of the bar-in this regard. Perhaps the most useful part of the report of the commissioner, however, is the catalogue of types of eavesdropping or interception of conversations which were engaged in in British Columbia.
The reason I feel I cannot accept the hon. member's bill-although I acknowledge that it is similar to a bill which was introduced at one time by my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell)-is that it is not adequate in this regard. I should like to refer my hon. friend to the excellent study made under the direction of Mr. Samuel Dash of Pennsylvania. The details of this are to be found in a book entitled "The Eavesdroppers". I believe Mr. Dash has presented much better than I could the particular criticism I
December 15, 19G7

would have of the hon. member's bill. At page 6 of "The Eavesdroppers" there appears this observation:
The failure of legislators to recognize the relationship among these eavesdropping techniques-
That is, telephonic interception and bugging.
-has led some states to enact strict prohibitions against one technique and completely overlook another. Thus, in Pennsylvania in 1957, it was made illegal for anyone to intercept a telephone communication, even for a law-enforcement purpose. The legislature ignored the use of concealed microphones, with the result that it is legal in Pennsylvania to bug a bedroom, den, or office, but illegal to intercept a telephone communication.
It seems to me that that captures the inadequacy of the hon. member's bill. While he is concerned about telephonic and telegraphic bugging he is not concerned about bugging of conference rooms or other more intimate places of meeting.
One of the more interesting things, as I have already said, was the reference made by Mr. Sargent to the very extensive use of bugging practices not only in the union field but also in industry and in other areas of Canada. Reference was made, for example, to the fact that in the automobile retail business it was not uncommon to use bugging devices to bug the conversations which may be taking place in the showrooms or in rooms adjacent to the showroom of automobile establishments. It was also established that an Arthur Murray dance studio in the province of British Columbia used a bugging device. The evidence was to the effect that it was used as a safety measure. The evidence discloses the enterprise which has been used in respect of bugging devices in the province of British Columbia. Reference is made to the fairly extensive monitoring practice carried on in jails. The hon. member referred to one type of monitoring. I would share his concern about the monitoring of telephone conversations when an accused is communicating with his counsel. However, in respect of monitoring devices in jails, to monitor the drunk tank so that the authorities may know whether there is a change in an individual's conduct which would suggest that treatment was necessary, or in respect of monitoring in maximum security institutions, I do not believe I can accept this.
However, the commissioner did refer to what he himself thought was extensive use of this type of equipment for industrial
Criminal Code
security. Unfortunately the report does not go into very much detail concerning the type of devices used or the type of situation in which they would be used. But apparently the commissioner did believe that this kind of electronic eavesdropping is used. The hon. member made reference to a situation in the city of Toronto, which I have the honour to represent. It is interesting that the Toronto Transportation Commission uses a type of television bugging device at the turnstiles of the St. George station so that they can find out who has been dropping tokens in the fare box and who has not been dropping tokens in the fare box.
Some of the comments of the commissioner and some of the comments I have made indicate that there is a wide spectrum of uses to which eavesdropping devices are put. Some of these I think would generally be recognized as being legitimate and others not. It is clear from the remarks that I have made that my reason for opposing the hon. member's bill-and this I am sure does not come with any great surprise to him-is the fact that he has not gone far enough in dealing with this kind of legal problem.
It might be interesting to have on the record some examples of the types of equipment and some indication of the scientific advance there has been in this area, as well as an indication of how subtle some of the types of equipment are. At page 30 of the commissioners's report we are given a number of examples. He pointed out that there are a great number of electronic devices now for sale and used in various situations. There is a sub-miniature FM transmitter known as the sugar lump. It is the world's smallest FM bug transmitter. It will pick up even whispers in a normal sized room. The transmission range is from 300 feet to more than one quarter mile. It can give a constant transmission for five days with a \\ ounce battery. Then the report goes on to refer to what are called spiked mikes, which I am sure is not intended as any assault on the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr). This appears at page 35 of the report as follows:
There is another contrivance, spike mikes, that look like needles. They go into the wall of the next room-about the size of a nail. It is not pushed quite through. The monitor on it is about as big as a thumb. They are equipped with small ear phones something like a stethoscope device.

Mr. Speaker, it would seem that this afternoon is the afternoon for the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) to get his lumps, although they are not exactly sugar lumps. This hon. member has said he anticipates a new section which will deal with wire tapping in the new proposed omnibus amendments to the Criminal Code to be presented soon, and that if there is no such provision in that bill he will have a great deal to say about that lack. Surely none of us can seriously expect that there will be such a provision in this omnibus bill to be presented shortly. We are not ready yet, I submit, for the introduction of such an amendment to the Criminal Code.
Let me say first that it would be only common sense to wait for the report of the royal commission on security, which has been sitting since about November of 1966. That report should be in our possession in the not too distant future. It is extremely likely that this report will make recommendations in respect of this particular subject. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) and the government should also have the benefit of the considered view on this whole subject by the Canadian Bar Association. We have just heard from the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) that this view or opinion will not be available until at least September or October of next year.
At this time there is authority in Canada for penitentiary officials to open letters either to or from inmates. There is also authorization here to search houses and other premises when a search warrant has been obtained. It would seem therefore that a parallel authorization to use electronic eavesdropping devices in certain cases should be provided. Under certain circumstances this would be in the public interest.
As pointed out by previous speakers we have at this time a variety of devices for eavesdropping such as sugar lumps and spike mikes, and other types of electronic listening
December 15, 1967

aids. We must explore this whole field in greater detail, using the best legal and technical minds available, before making any decision as to the type of legislation we require.
It may be of interest to hon. members to consider a bill relating to wire tapping which was introduced in Congress by the attorney general of the United States in 1964. The purpose of the bill is stated as one-
-to afford a clear cut basis for the legitimate and controlled use of wire tapping by law enforcement officials.
The attorney general suggested this should be so, while expressly forbidding all other types of wire tapping.
Criminal Code
Speaking before the Senate subcommittee on organized crime and illicit traffic in narcotics, the attorney general said:
Section 5(b) of this bill empowers the attorney general, or an assistant attorney general specially designated by the attorney general to authorize application to a federal judge for a wiretap order.
